facts.content: Patient reports shortness of breath and a sensation of lip and tongue swelling after a bee or wasp sting minutes ago.
facts.source_text: CC: SOB and lip/tongue swelling sensation after bee/wasp sting minutes ago

facts.content: The patient was stung on the arm minutes prior to presentation.
facts.source_text: HPI: Sting to arm minutes prior;

facts.content: There is a localized rash and erythema with a puncture mark at the sting site.
The rash is described as blotchy.
There is no obvious swelling at the sting site reported in the history.
Earlier the patient felt mild shortness of breath but is currently breathing okay.
facts.source_text: earlier felt mild SOB; currently breathing OK;

facts.content: The patient is anxious about the reaction worsening.
The patient has a history of eczema.
The patient has intermittent anxiety or panic without having been on medications.
The patient has no history of anaphylaxis.
The patient is allergic to penicillin.
The patient works as a computer scientist.
The patient lives alone.
The patient has a cat.
The patient reports no known pet or food allergies.
facts.source_text: no known pet or food allergies

facts.content: The patient is speaking in full sentences with no apparent respiratory distress on video.
facts.source_text: General: Speaking in full sentences; no apparent resp distress on video

facts.content: The lips are not visibly swollen on examination.
The oropharynx visualized via video shows no visible soft tissue swelling.
facts.source_text: OP visualized via video—no visible soft tissue swelling;

facts.content: The patient has normal phonation.
Breathing appears normal to the examiner.
facts.source_text: Resp: Breathing appears normal to examiner

facts.content: The arm sting site shows mild erythema and a puncture mark with no obvious swelling.
facts.source_text: Skin: Arm sting site with mild erythema and puncture mark; no obvious swelling

facts.content: Vital signs were not obtained.

The clinician assesses a localized allergic reaction to a bee or wasp sting occurring minutes after the sting with mild localized erythema and no current airway compromise and low suspicion for anaphylaxis.
facts.source_text: 1) Localized allergic reaction to bee/wasp sting—minutes post-sting; mild localized erythema; no current airway compromise; low suspicion for anaphylaxis

facts.content: The clinician assesses anxiety related to the sting.
The patient is advised to take over-the-counter chlorphenamine (Piriton) 4 mg up to six times per day or a once-daily over-the-counter antihistamine.
facts.source_text: Antihistamine: OTC chlorphenamine (Piriton) 4 mg up to 6×/day, or a once-daily OTC antihistamine

facts.content: The patient is instructed to return or go to the emergency department if lip or tongue swelling, shortness of breath, stridor, or rapid progression occurs.
facts.source_text: Safety-net: Return/ED if lip/tongue swelling, SOB, stridor, or rapid progression

facts.content: The patient is advised to monitor the sting site and, if spreading erythema, warmth, or signs of local infection develop, to assess the need for antibiotics.
facts.source_text: Monitor sting site; if spreading erythema/warmth or signs of local infection, assess need for abx

facts.content: No allergy testing is planned now, but it may be considered if recurrent reactions or rashes occur.
facts.source_text: No allergy testing now; consider if recurrent reactions/rashes

facts.content: The patient will be provided written information on anaphylaxis and is encouraged to re-contact with concerns.
facts.source_text: Provide written info on anaphylaxis; encourage re-contact with concerns
